method: violentCrime.scale = 0.5 x D + 0.5 x B, the two parts weighted equally because in the United States the 1.2 micromorts a person (x $14.6 x 2.5 people = $44) and the $40 of loss carry about equal weight. D, the deaths ratio, is the UNODC intentional-homicide rate (latest year, read from the Wikipedia table built on UNODC data) divided by the US rate of the same year (2024: 5.0, FBI; 2023: 5.76, UNODC; 2020-22 recalled), times s, the share of homicide committed in robbery or burglary relative to the US share (about 9%: NVDRS robbery 6.5% + burglary 2.5%). s is 0.7 for rich low-homicide countries (England and Wales: 6% of homicides in furtherance of theft or gain, ONS), 0.85 for South Africa (SAPS: robbery 382 of 5,596 murders with a known factor), about 0.25 for Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, where gang and cartel killing dominates (Brazil: 807 latrocinio victims among 40,775 violent deaths in 2025), and a guess elsewhere. B, the loss ratio, is household burglary frequency relative to the US times L, the loss per burglary in dollars relative to the US. In Europe frequency is Eurostat's police-recorded burglary of private homes per 100,000 (mean of 2022-24) over the US police-recorded figure (about 140: 779,542 burglaries in 2024, about 60% residential, which matches the NCVS 8.2 per 1,000 households at a 45% reporting rate), times 0.6 for the higher reporting of insured European households (0.75 in central, eastern and southern Europe); L = 1. Elsewhere frequency comes from victim surveys (South Africa's housebreaking 5.9% and home robbery 1.1% of households against the US 0.71%) or is a guess, and L is 0.45-0.65 for upper-middle-income and 0.2-0.3 for lower-middle-income countries (goods, repairs and time cost fewer dollars). Ranges take the 5th and 95th percentiles of s and B together. civilUnrest follows the anchors: list the episodes since 1990 that meet the threshold (riot curfew or state of siege, serious rioting or looting, disorder sustained over days, or armed conflict on home territory, including missile and rocket fire on cities and cartel or insurgent violence that shuts a city down), give each the share of the country's urban population living in the cities it touched, as the US anchor counts whole cities under curfew, sum, and divide by the years; the forecast leans towards the rate of the last ten to fifteen years and present conditions (Verisk Maplecroft's ranking, elections and wars in the next year); the pessimistic figure is two to three times the forecast, as for the anchors, or the recent peak rate where that is higher. Episodes come from Wikipedia's List of riots and event pages I fetched; population shares are my estimates.

My components are close to the preset researcher's (mortality 0.12 against 0.2, loss 0.85 against 1.0), but blending them with equal weight gives 0.5; the preset's 0.4 implies a weight of about three quarters on deaths, which I could not trace. 0.4 lies inside my range. reproduced.basis: Anchor's own count: 92 million person-episodes (1967-68, 1992, 2020, others) over 62 years x 260 million = 0.6% a year, 1.5% in 2015-26. Adding the downtown Los Angeles curfew of June 2025 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_riots) changes nothing at this precision.

A 2020-sized wave (18% of residents) every six years; Verisk Maplecroft ranks the US fifth in the world and first among Western democracies for riot risk in 2026 (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/international/2026/02/17/858246.htm).

With the anchor's weights (France 4%, England 1%, elsewhere 0.3%) the population-weighted figure is 1.0%. With my country figures (France 5% after the October 2026 riots and curfews, UK 1.3% with Northern Ireland, the others 0.15-1.2%) it is 1.3%.

openQuestions: The engine applies one violentCrime scale to both micromorts and dollars. Deaths and losses differ by country far more than either does from the blend (South Africa D 6.8, B 3.8; France D 0.19, B 1.25). Each country's notes give D and B; splitting the field into a mortality scale and a loss scale would let the engine value deaths at the country's micromortValueUsd without distorting losses.
My equal-weight blend gives 0.5 for Western Europe against the preset's 0.4. If the owner keeps 0.4, my European figures should be multiplied by about 0.8 to stay on the preset's scale.

Israel's civilUnrest (35%) is war, not riot: the Western Europe preset's windows and its 2% conflict share understate shelter days and school closures and overstate looting. The same holds, less starkly, for cartel and insurgent violence in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil and Nigeria under the Buenos Aires preset's 1% conflict share.

For Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Finland, Korea, Japan and China part of civilUnrest is attack by a foreign state, which overlaps greatPowerWar (and nuclear hazards); the engine may count it twice.
Police-recorded burglary definitions differ: Slovakia, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia come out implausibly low against western Europe and may count only flats or only completed break-ins.
The loss factor L (0.2-0.65 outside rich countries) is my guess at how far stolen goods, repairs and time cost fewer dollars; the prices family's priceIndex and timeValueUsdPerHour could replace it.
